signal.name: TGF-β3
signal.note: Working signal since 2026-11-05: anti-scarring in a phase II trial ({cite:mccollum2011avotermin}) and less activating than TGF-β1 in fibroblasts ({cite:urban2023isoforms}). The model is signal-agnostic; the choice is confirmed with the group's secretome and RNA-seq data.

groups.title: Whose skin
groups.note: The dermis you are injecting into. The basic model (age, sex, body site) sets the advanced values from measurements; change an advanced value and it stays yours. The badge on each value says how well it is known. The senescent share is part of the tissue and follows the age.

groups.title: What the cells make
groups.note: What the implanted cells secrete and what it takes to answer it. This is where the answer is decided, and where the uncertainty is.

groups.title: How you inject
groups.note: Your design: where the sites go and how much goes into each.

groups.title: How much it varies
groups.note: Patients differ, and so does tissue within one patient. These values drive the Robustness analysis: many random tissues, and how often the design reaches its target. They do not change the maps.

groups.title: The device
groups.note: Only for the injection scaffold: what the needle array would look like.

groups.title: What you look at
groups.note: Where and when you are looking. Changes nothing about the design.

parameters.label: Dermis thickness (model)
parameters.note: Default: the 2-mm-deep dermal region of the reconstructed skin model ({cite:roy2024implanting}). Human dermis is thicker at most trunk sites — papillary plus reticular comes to 2.7 mm periumbilical in donors over 55 ({cite:arnalforne2024dermis}) and 2.4–2.9 mm on abdomen and back by 50 MHz ultrasound ({cite:wang2025ultrasound}). The body site and sex of the basic model set it from the ultrasound study; the skin model is the default site.

parameters.label: Aged-cell threshold factor s_age
parameters.note: Aged cells respond blunted or divergently ({cite:liao2026chromatin}): the direction is sourced, the size of the factor is a placeholder. The aged-cell threshold is c_on × s_age.

parameters.label: Dermis model
parameters.note: How the dermis is modelled. 2, depth-resolved (the default): diffusion is slower near the dermal–epidermal junction and clearance follows the local fibroblast density — the measured picture — and the signal is solved in depth through that profile. 1, averaged per level: the same dermis, but each injection level sees one average diffusion coefficient and decay length; faster, and wrong where a source reaches the papillary dermis (kept for comparison, and it is what the viewer showed up to 0.9). 0, uniform: one diffusion coefficient and one decay length through the whole dermis, the model up to M2, and what the analytic check is done against. See {help:model/layers|A dermis with depth}.

parameters.label: Epidermis thickness
parameters.note: Used by the injection scaffold: the model measures depth below the dermal–epidermal junction, a needle from the skin surface. Default: 75 µm, the dorsal forearm of 71 volunteers (stratum corneum 18.3 ± 4.9 µm plus cellular epidermis 56.6 ± 11.5 µm, {cite:sandbymoller2003epidermis}). The face is thinner, 29.6–62.6 µm across 39 subunits ({cite:chopra2015face}); the abdomen measures 110 ± 18 µm by ultrasound ({cite:wang2025ultrasound}). Body site explains most of the variation: the body site of the basic model sets it, by the pooled values of a meta-analysis of histology, optical coherence tomography and confocal microscopy for that site and age; ultrasound reads the epidermis too thick and is not used ({cite:lintzeri2022epidermis}). See {help:scaffold/needles|Needle lengths}.

parameters.label: Papillary dermis thickness
parameters.note: Depth of the papillary dermis, the denser-celled upper layer. Default: 101.2 ± 21.4 µm, measured on photoprotected periumbilical skin of donors aged 58–79 (the study's group of 55 and over) — the age group this project is about; the same study gives 71–77 µm below 55 and a reticular dermis of 2.6–3.8 mm ({cite:arnalforne2024dermis}). Post-auricular skin of men around 68 gave 133 ± 22 µm ({cite:hachmo2021papillary}). The papillary dermis is thus a few per cent of the dermis, not the 20 % that ultrasound reviews assume. What it is: the histological band of thin collagen bundles beneath the dermal–epidermal junction in fixed autopsy skin, not the depth to the subpapillary vascular plexus (330 ± 26 µm in four biopsies, {cite:pedrazzani2020lcoct}), about four times deeper. Caveat, the age trend is contested: histology finds it thicker with age (the same group, 45 autopsies: +0.36 µm per year, R² = 0.26, {cite:marcosgarces2014collagen}; both attribute it to water and GAG, not to more fibres), whereas in vivo intensity-profile OCT finds it thinner, 94.4 → 52.4 µm on the cheek from 22–27 to 61–69 y ({cite:pedrazzani2020lcoct}) and 63.75 → 30.75 µm on the sun-protected upper arm from 20–39 to 60–79 y ({cite:boone2015hdoct}); 150 MHz ultrasound with OCT finds no change ({cite:querleux2009ethnic}). Site and sun exposure do not explain it (the protected upper arm thins too); the measurement does. The value is the histological one and stays; see docs/papillary-dermis-thickness.md (claims L22 to L29).

parameters.label: Papillary cell density
parameters.note: How many times more cells the papillary dermis holds than the reticular. It matters because uptake by cells, not chemistry, is what removes the signal: niche size scales with the density of consuming cells ({cite:oyleryaniv2017niches}). Default: 2714 ± 451 against 247 ± 86 cells/mm² of section in donors aged 55 and over ({cite:arnalforne2024dermis}), a ratio of 11. Two caveats: those are *all* nuclei, not fibroblasts only, and they are per mm² of a section, so the ratio carries over to a volume density only if the section thickness is the same for both layers. For scale, mid-dermis holds 2100–4100 fibroblasts/mm³ in young donors ({cite:miller2003density}).

parameters.label: Diffusion at the junction
parameters.note: Diffusion is slowest right under the epidermis: 0.7–3 µm²/s at the dermal–epidermal junction against 1–20 µm²/s deeper in the dermis ({cite:wei2018microneedle}). What happens deeper is contested: one study found papillary and reticular dermis to differ only marginally ({cite:romgens2015diffusion}), two others a rise of about an order of magnitude towards the reticular dermis ({cite:wei2018microneedle}, {cite:raphael2013depth}); in Wei's analysis that rise (10–20 µm²/s) is the 2D Cartesian model's result only, while the axisymmetric model stays at about 1–3 µm²/s in the dermis, so it depends on the fitting geometry (claim T3). The model follows the first and puts the whole depth dependence of D into this junction zone, which is the conservative choice.

parameters.label: Depth of the slow zone
parameters.note: Over this depth D rises from its junction value to the bulk value, D(z) = D − (D − D_junction)·e^(−z/this). That diffusion is slowest at the junction is measured ({cite:wei2018microneedle}); how thick the zone is was not found, so the depth itself is a placeholder.

parameters.label: Cellularity (relative)
parameters.note: How many cells the dermis holds, relative to the default tissue (donors aged 55 and over), for which λ is the decay length. Uptake by cells is what removes the signal, and it follows the density of consuming cells ({cite:oyleryaniv2017niches}), so more cells mean a shorter λ and fewer a longer one. The age of the basic model sets it from total cell counts per mm² of section in four age groups ({cite:arnalforne2024dermis}) — all nuclei, not fibroblasts only, hence an analogue. See {help:model/age|Age of the skin}.

parameters.label: Senescent share of host cells
parameters.note: Share of the host cells that are senescent. They are not counted as targets (coverage is over the others) and, with the SASP factor below, they raise the threshold around them. In human dermis, p21-positive cells increased with age and made up to 15 % of cells in donors over 65, while p16 was almost undetectable ({cite:idda2020senescence}); in baboon skin, dermal fibroblasts with damaged telomeres reached over 15 % of all fibroblasts ({cite:jeyapalan2007primates}; the same finding in {cite:herbig2006primates}). Two human-skin full texts support the direction only: p16-positive dermal cells per field rise from 0.0 to 3.1 to 8.2 with age ({cite:ressler2006p16}) and SA-β-gal staining of the dermis appears in all but one donor over 69 y and in none under 40 y ({cite:dimri1995biomarker}); neither gives a share of cells, so the magnitude rests on Idda alone (claim A16). Markers of senescence in all cells, not a count of senescent fibroblasts: an analogue. The age of the basic model sets it, scaled by how p21-positive dermal cells rise with age (our mapping of the age groups, claim K4). It belongs to the tissue, so it is set here; it acts in the Robustness analysis, which leaves senescent cells out of the targets and lets them shift the threshold around them. The maps of the average tissue do not change with it.

parameters.label: Below the dermis
parameters.note: What happens at the deep side of the dermis, the hypodermis. 0, open: the dermis simply continues — the model up to M3, and the middle case, in which below H the signal is cleared as in the dermis. 1, absorbing: the deep vascular plexus at the dermal–subcutaneous junction ({cite:braverman1997microcirculation}) clears everything that reaches it. 2, closed: nothing passes into the fat. No measurement says which holds; 1 and 2 bracket 0. It matters only for sites within a few λ of the dermis thickness. See {help:model/deep|Below the dermis}.

parameters.label: Active secretion per cell
parameters.note: Secretion of the **active** (signalling) form by one implanted cell — fibroblasts release TGF-β almost entirely as a latent complex, so this is a small fraction of what an ELISA of conditioned medium measures. Built from two checked steps. *Total:* ≈ 0.4 ng/10⁶ cells/day — ≤ 15 pg/10⁶ cells/h uninduced in human fetal lung fibroblasts ({cite:kelley1993autoinduction}), and 4.8 ± 0.8 pg/10⁴ cells in human dermal fibroblast medium by ELISA ({cite:ghahary1998igf1}), whose collection interval is not in the abstract, so 0.16–0.48 ng/day. *Active share:* ≤ 2 % at baseline in primary human dermal fibroblasts, 11 % once they contract and 36 % in dermal myofibroblasts ({cite:klingberg2014prestress}). 0.4 ng/day × 2 % ≈ 8 pg/10⁶ cells/day; a contractile implanted cell would give about 40. Nothing is known about rejuvenated cells ({cite:hanasono2003fibroblasts} has the right design for dermal fibroblasts but no numbers in its abstract). A threshold can be expressed in the same unit ({cite:ozawa2004vegf}).

parameters.label: Activation threshold c_on (young cells)
parameters.note: Concentration at which young fibroblasts respond, and the EC50 of the graded response. Default: 1 ng/mL, which induced SMAD2 phosphorylation and α-SMA protein in primary human knee fibroblasts ({cite:dilger2025concentration}) and raised proliferation of nasal-polyp fibroblasts ({cite:serpero2006polyp}) — both analogues, not dermal cells, and a lowest effective dose rather than a fitted EC50. See {help:model/window|The therapeutic window}.

parameters.label: Fibrotic ceiling c_fib
parameters.note: Above this, conversion to myofibroblasts is expected. Default: 10 ng/mL, the lower of the two doses (10 and 20 ng/mL) that raised α-SMA in nasal-polyp fibroblasts while 1 ng/mL did not ({cite:serpero2006polyp}). Collagen deposition itself showed no upper limit from 0.5 to 40 ng/mL ({cite:dilger2025concentration}), so this ceiling is the myofibroblast switch, not a loss of effect. Analogues, not dermal cells. Windows with an upper side are documented for other signals, e.g. CCN2 ({cite:nakerakanti2011ccn2}).

parameters.label: Effective decay length λ
parameters.note: How far the signal carries before uptake, capture and degradation remove it. Default: the upper end of 80–120 µm measured for cytokines in dense tissue in vivo ({cite:oyleryaniv2017niches}), an analogous system, not TGF-β itself. A single cell communicates within about 250 µm ({cite:francis1997distances}). Diffusion and chemical clearance alone would give about 1.6 mm (our calculation from {cite:romgens2015diffusion} and {cite:sprugel1987kinetics}). See {help:model/lambda|Decay length λ}.

parameters.label: Diffusion coefficient D
parameters.note: Measured in human dermis for a 40 kDa tracer ({cite:romgens2015diffusion}); other tracers gave 1–20 µm²/s ({cite:wei2018microneedle}). TGF-β dimers are smaller than 40 kDa, so the default is likely conservative.

parameters.label: Hill exponent n
parameters.note: Steepness of the graded dose response R(c) = cⁿ / (EC50ⁿ + cⁿ), with EC50 = the aged-cell threshold, so the response is half-maximal there. No fitted Hill exponent for TGF-β on fibroblasts was found; 1 (no cooperativity) is the neutral placeholder. Short-term SMAD2 phosphorylation is graded while the long-term response is switch-like ({cite:zi2011dynamics}), so n > 1 is likely for a late readout — the direction is sourced, the number is not. See {help:model/response|Graded response}.

parameters.label: Implant half-life t½
parameters.note: Time over which half of the signalling implanted cells are lost or stop secreting. No measured half-life was found, only brackets: labelled fibroblasts injected into rabbit dermis were still detectable at 56 days, with a rise and fall in the first 28 days ({cite:hebda1999transplanted}); allogeneic fibroblasts were rejected within a week in immunocompetent mice ({cite:farrokhi2022rejection}); in patients the healing effect of one injection was gone after 28 days ({cite:petrof2013erosions}). The group analysed its implants after 10 days and saw matrix deposition decline after 2–3 divisions ({cite:roy2024implanting}). Placeholder inside those brackets; it scales the whole time course.

parameters.label: Chemical half-life in tissue
parameters.note: Half-life of the signal where no cell takes it up; 22 h for ¹²⁵I-TGF-β in subcutaneous collagen chambers ({cite:sprugel1987kinetics}). With the decay length λ it splits the decay into a chemical part and an uptake part — for the default values more than 99 % is uptake — and only the uptake part follows the cell density with depth. See {help:model/layers|A dermis with depth}.

parameters.label: Molecular weight
parameters.note: Only converts between ng/mL, pM and molecules. Placeholder (mature TGF-β dimer assumed) until sourced.

parameters.label: Site spacing
parameters.note: Distance between neighbouring sites of the lattice (random pattern: same mean density as the hexagonal lattice).

parameters.label: Cells per site
parameters.note: Default: the group's protocol, spheroids equivalent to 40,000 cells per site ({cite:roy2024implanting}).

parameters.label: Injection depth (middle level)
parameters.note: Design choice: depth of the middle injection level below the dermal–epidermal junction. The group implanted within the 2-mm-deep dermis of the skin model ({cite:roy2024implanting}).

parameters.label: Injection depths (levels)
parameters.note: Number of injection depths. With more than one, each depth is a lattice of the same spacing, shifted sideways against its neighbours, so that seen from above the sites are closer together while in depth they keep their distance. See {help:model/depths|Several injection depths}.

parameters.label: Spacing between depths
parameters.note: Vertical distance between neighbouring injection depths (used with more than one depth). All depths are kept inside the dermis.

parameters.label: Cluster radius
parameters.note: Radius of the sphere of implanted cells. Placeholder geometry; implanted cells also spread over days.

parameters.label: Target coverage C*
parameters.note: The share of the (non-senescent) host cells a design must put inside the window for one realisation to count as a success. Robustness is the share of realisations that succeed, P(C ≥ C*).

parameters.label: Overexposure limit O*
parameters.note: The share of the host cells that may lie above the fibrotic ceiling in a successful realisation. A realisation succeeds when C ≥ C* and O ≤ O*, the plan's definition of an ideal density; 5 % is the plan's example.

parameters.label: Required robustness P*
parameters.note: How often a design must succeed to count as robust. Along the optimiser's front, the robust ideal density is the cheapest design that succeeds in at least this share of the random tissues.

parameters.label: Spread of the insertion depth
parameters.note: How much the share of the needle length that enters the skin varies from one application to the next; each realisation draws one application, and all its deposits move deeper or shallower together. Sharp needles entered 64–90 % of their height ({cite:cordeiro2020templates}); 600 µm needles reached 330 µm at 4.4 N and 520 µm at 16.4 N per array ({cite:donnelly2010geometry}). Default: the standard deviation of an even spread over 64–90 % (our derivation), in skin models and pig skin rather than aged human skin, hence an analogue.

parameters.label: Donor spread, papillary cellularity
parameters.note: How much the papillary cellularity differs between donors of one age group: 2714 ± 450.50 cells/mm² of section at 55 and over ({cite:arnalforne2024dermis}, n = 5). Each realisation draws one donor from a log-normal with this coefficient of variation. All nuclei, not fibroblasts only; the age of the basic model sets it for its group.

parameters.label: Donor spread, reticular cellularity
parameters.note: The same for the reticular dermis: 246.50 ± 85.72 cells/mm² of section at 55 and over ({cite:arnalforne2024dermis}, n = 5).

parameters.label: Donor spread, papillary thickness
parameters.note: The same for the papillary thickness: 101.2 ± 21.43 µm at 55 and over ({cite:arnalforne2024dermis}, n = 5).

parameters.label: Cell-to-cell spread of the threshold
parameters.note: Single cells answer the same dose differently: a cell's threshold is the median × e^(this × a standard normal draw). Single-cell responses to TGF-β are set cell by cell by the levels of signalling proteins ({cite:strasen2018variability}), and fibroblast responses were heterogeneous ({cite:urban2023isoforms}); the size of the spread is not given there. Placeholder, off by default.

parameters.label: SASP effect on the threshold
parameters.note: Senescent cells secrete a mixture of factors (the SASP, {cite:coppe2008sasp}). Here the threshold of a host cell is multiplied by 1 + this × senescent share × local cell density. Positive: the SASP blunts the response, as the project plan assumed. But the SASP also carries TGF-β family ligands that induce senescence in neighbouring cells ({cite:acosta2013paracrine}), so it may act with the signal rather than against it — negative values. Neither size nor sign is measured: placeholder, off by default.

parameters.label: Variation of cell density within the dermis
parameters.note: Local variation of the cell density beyond the two layers: a random field (log-normal, mean 1) with this coefficient of variation and the correlation length below, scaling the uptake around each implant site and weighting the host cells. Not measured; placeholder, off by default.

parameters.label: Variation of diffusion within the dermis
parameters.note: Local variation of the diffusion coefficient, as a second random field. FRAP in human skin found only marginal variation within and between papillary and reticular dermis ({cite:romgens2015diffusion}); the size of the local variation is not given. Placeholder, off by default.

parameters.label: Correlation length of the variation
parameters.note: How far apart two points must be to vary independently, for both random fields. Not measured; placeholder.

parameters.label: Realisations
parameters.note: Random tissues per run (each a donor, its random fields and its host cells). The panel reports the standard errors, so you can see whether this is enough.

parameters.label: Host cells per realisation
parameters.note: Host cells sampled per realisation. Their sampling noise is part of each realisation's coverage; more cells, less noise, more time.

parameters.label: Needle outer diameter
parameters.note: Outer diameter of one needle at the skin surface, drawn in the layout and written into the specification. Design choice, not a model value: reported hollow needles carry a 10–40 µm cannula ({cite:burton2011hmts}) and solid tips of 5–37 µm needed 20–167 mN to insert, rising with tip diameter ({cite:romgens2014tip}). See {help:scaffold/spec|What the fabricator gets}.

parameters.label: Penetration of needle length
parameters.note: A needle does not enter the skin to its full length, because the skin is pressed in with it, so the needle has to be longer than the target depth: length = (epidermis + depth) / this factor. Default 0.8: sharp conical and pyramidal arrays inserted to 64–90 % of needle height ({cite:cordeiro2020templates}); 600 µm needles reached 330 µm at 4.4 N and 520 µm at 16.4 N per array ({cite:donnelly2010geometry}) — so it depends on the application force, and both are polymeric arrays in skin models, not hollow needles in human dermis.

parameters.label: Scaffold patch size
parameters.note: Edge length of the square patch of skin the scaffold covers. Decides how many needles the array has; the layout itself is the periodic tile repeated over this area. For scale, a reported hollow-microneedle device is 1.27 cm² with 18 needles ({cite:burton2011hmts}).

parameters.label: Time after implantation
parameters.note: Everything shown is the steady state of the implant as it is on this day: the source per site is scaled by the surviving fraction S(t) = 2^(−t/t½). 0 is the fresh implant. See {help:model/time|Time after implantation}.

parameters.label: Slice depth (en-face map)
parameters.note: Depth of the en-face map below the dermal–epidermal junction. Follows the injection depth until you move it.

parameters.label: Cross-section position
parameters.note: Where the cross-section cuts the en-face map (dashed line).

parameters.label: Field of view
parameters.note: Width of the en-face map.

presets.note: Layers and cells from photoprotected periumbilical skin, 25 autopsies in four age groups; total cellularity is all nuclei per mm² of section ({cite:arnalforne2024dermis}, Table 5). The senescent share from p21-positive dermal cells in three groups of skin donors ({cite:idda2020senescence}). Only the tissue changes; the signal, the thresholds and the design stay as they are.
presets.derivation: **How the six groups were derived.** The age cut-offs of every age-resolved study in the project were laid over each other, and a cut was kept where studies of several quantities agree; no cut-off was moved. **12 | 13** and **25 | 26** are the group borders of the one histology study that measured the papillary dermis and the cell counts by age ({cite:arnalforne2024dermis}); growth of the skin ends at about 20 years ({cite:tan1982ultrasound}, {cite:diridollou2001ageing}). **39 | 40** is where the studies of senescent cells ({cite:idda2020senescence}, {cite:dimri1995biomarker}), of the superficial dermis by optical imaging ({cite:pedrazzani2020lcoct}, {cite:boone2015hdoct}) and of the dermis by ultrasound ({cite:wang2023density}) set a border. **54 | 55** is again the histology study's border ({cite:arnalforne2024dermis}). **69 | 70** is where p16-positive dermal cells jump ({cite:ressler2006p16}), where senescence staining separates the old donors ({cite:dimri1995biomarker}), where cell counts are binned ({cite:andrew1964dermis}, {cite:gunin2011dermis}) and about where ultrasound shows the skin thinning ({cite:derigal1989ultrasound}, {cite:escoffier1989mechanical}). **Further series**, read after the groups were set, move none of these borders. Ultrasound finds the whole skin unchanged from 27 to 70 years and thinner after ({cite:lasagni1995echographic}), thinner over 60 than at 27–31 years at most sites with few of the differences significant ({cite:seidenari1994echography}), and the dermis of the arm within 6 % between four age groups ({cite:crisan2012ultrasound}). Children aged 2–13 have 78 % of the forearm skin thickness of adults aged 25–40 ({cite:seidenari2000children}), which is what the growth line used here gives. **The forehead** has a line of its own. Nine ultrasound series give the thickness of forehead skin by age: thinner with age in five ({cite:denda1990facial}, {cite:seidenari1994echography}, {cite:wang2023density}, {cite:meng2022facial}, {cite:jeong2023facial}), unchanged in two ({cite:lasagni1995echographic}, {cite:korzekwa2025face}), thicker in two ({cite:takema1994facial}, {cite:pellacani1999facial}). On the face the loss of dermis with age runs against what sunlight adds to the upper dermis, and the lower border of the dermis is hard to find by ultrasound ({cite:pellacani1999facial}). The model follows the largest series by decade, whose regression for each sex is used from 20 to 70 years ({cite:denda1990facial}); sun damage has no value in the model. The share of type III collagen is constant from 14 to 65 years and rises after ({cite:lovell1987collagen}). The transcriptome of skin fibroblasts clusters into the ages 1–15, 16–26, 27–60, 61–85 and 86–96 years ({cite:braunger2024aging}): beside the two young borders, silent on the others. **What each group rests on.** Papillary thickness and cell counts were measured in donors aged 0.1–2, 13–25, 34–54 and 58–79 years, five to ten each, and are published as group means only ({cite:arnalforne2024dermis}); p21-positive dermal cells in skin donors aged 19–30, 41–46 and 70–90 years, five each ({cite:idda2020senescence}). A group mean is placed at the mean age of its donors (the middle of their age range where only the range is published) and the means are joined by straight lines; beyond the youngest and the oldest mean the value is held, never extrapolated. Each group is evaluated at one age: 13–25 at 18.6 years and 40–54 at 42.9 years, the mean ages of the donors measured in them, 70 and over at 80 years, the middle of the oldest skin donors; 0–12, 26–39 and 55–69 hold no group mean, so they are evaluated at their middle (6, 32.5 and 62 years) and their values are interpolated. No donor was aged 3–12 or 26–33 years, and none over 79 years for the layers. An independent count of fibroblast-like cells is constant from the second decade to 71–85 years ({cite:gunin2011dermis}); it counts a different thing and is not used. A second histology series of the same department gives the papillary thickness as a regression on age, 63.24 µm at birth and 0.361 µm more per year, and the reticular thickness as a curve with its maximum in mid-life ({cite:marcosgarces2014collagen}); both are shown beside the values for comparison and not used, because imaging of living skin finds the superficial dermis thinner with age, not thicker ({cite:pedrazzani2020lcoct}, {cite:boone2015hdoct}). **An age in years** takes the same lines at that age and adds one regression: the skin thickness of the forearm by ultrasound, falling by 0.0036 mm per year in men and 0.002 mm in women over 21 years and rising by 0.019 mm per year up to 20 years ({cite:tan1982ultrasound}; a second ultrasound study found 0.004 and 0.003 mm per year, {cite:escoffier1989mechanical}). It scales the dermis thickness of a measured body site from the median age of that site's volunteers (30 years for the men, 45 for the women, {cite:wang2025ultrasound}) to the chosen age; the growth line is used as a shape and joined to the adult line at 20 years (our construction). Histology of the inner arm gives a steeper loss, 12.8 µm per year ({cite:branchet1990thickness}), and the rate differs by site ({cite:wang2023density}), so the forearm line is an analogue for the other sites. **The epidermis** of a body site is not taken from that ultrasound table: ultrasound reads the epidermis systematically thicker than histology, optical coherence tomography and confocal microscopy, and a meta-analysis of 142 studies advises against it ({cite:lintzeri2022epidermis}). The model takes the pooled values of that meta-analysis, a younger and an older group of studies per skin area with their mean ages, joined by a straight line and held beyond (forearm: 80.6 µm at 27 and 63.6 µm at 60 years), the same for both sexes. The chest comes from the two groups of one imaging study ({cite:gambichler2006epidermis}); the dorsum of the foot has one pooled value for all ages. What thins is the mean over the dermal–epidermal junction, because the rete ridges retract; the plate above the papillae keeps its thickness ({cite:neerken2004oct}, {cite:sauermann2002clsm}). That is why the series disagree: one histology series found it thinning ({cite:branchet1990thickness}), another none between 20 and 68 years ({cite:sandbymoller2003epidermis}); optical coherence tomography finds it 9 to 15 µm thinner at 60–80 than at 20–40 years at six sites ({cite:gambichler2006epidermis}), ultrasound unchanged ({cite:crisan2012ultrasound}), which resolves some 50 µm in depth and cannot see a change of this size. A larger histology series finds the thinning too ({cite:waaijer2012morphometric}). The collagen area fraction by age is shown from its published regressions ({cite:marcosgarces2014collagen}); no value of the model takes it.

sites.note: Dermis by very-high-frequency ultrasound in 74 healthy adults (41 men, 33 women) at West China Hospital ({cite:wang2025ultrasound}). The dermis was thicker in men except on the back. The epidermis is not taken from this table, because ultrasound reads it too thick: it comes from a meta-analysis of other methods, by site and age, and does not depend on the sex ({cite:lintzeri2022epidermis}). Two other ultrasound studies also found the dermis thicker in men at most sites ({cite:wang2023density}, {cite:firooz2017echodensity}), and two more the whole skin ({cite:lasagni1995echographic}, {cite:seidenari1994echography}). The sex sets the dermis thickness and nothing else. Dermal cells differed only slightly or negligibly between men and women ({cite:quaglino1996dermis}), and no checked source gives the cell density, the papillary thickness or the senescent share by sex. Women have the denser dermis — a higher volume fraction of collagen fibres except in the second and third decades of life ({cite:vitellaro1994stereology}) and a higher echo density ({cite:firooz2017echodensity}, {cite:wang2023density}) — with less collagen in total ({cite:shuster1975collagen}), and in women the collagen follows the years since the menopause more than the age ({cite:brincat1985thickness}, {cite:castelobranco1992hrt}, {cite:affinito1999hypoestrogenism}); no value of the model takes that. The skin model is the group's reconstructed aged skin, 2 mm of dermis ({cite:roy2024implanting}), with the forearm epidermis of a histology study ({cite:sandbymoller2003epidermis}); it is the same for both sexes. **The face and neck.** Twelve facial areas and the neck come from a second ultrasound study, which gives the dermis by sex at 19 sites of head and neck in 20 men and 20 women aged 15–76 years ({cite:hoffmann1994sonography}); its forehead agrees with the site table's within 10 %, so the facial areas sit on the same scale as the body sites. Its dermis is scaled with age from the median ages of its own volunteers (32 years for the men, 47 for the women): the cheek by its own regression, the upper face by the forehead's, the lower face by the cheek's ({cite:denda1990facial}). Other ultrasound series find the facial dermis about half as thick ({cite:meng2022facial}, {cite:jeong2023facial}); the order of the areas agrees, the level does not. The epidermis of an area is the forehead's or the cheek's at that age ({cite:lintzeri2022epidermis}) times the ratio of the area to it in one histology series of 39 facial subunits ({cite:chopra2015face}). No source gives the cell density, the papillary dermis or the senescent share by facial area; they follow the age as at every body site.

ethnicity.note: The groups under which the sources' labels fall (Caucasian, French, German; Chinese, Japanese, Korean; Thai; Indian; Turkish, Iranian; African American, African; Mexican, Brazilian, Hispanic). The dermis thickness does not differ between ethnic groups measured the same way ({cite:querleux2009ethnic}, {cite:whitmore2000caliper}, {cite:mercurio2016brazilian}), nor does the papillary dermis below the papillae ({cite:querleux2009ethnic}); cell density and senescent share were never measured by group. The one difference in a model value that the skin type does not explain is the facial epidermis of East Asian skin, thicker at the cheekbone by the same method ({cite:assi2024asian}, against {cite:bonnier2023lcoct}): the choice East Asian sets the epidermis of the cheek; every other choice sets nothing. European is the default because most of the model's sources measured European skin.

phototype.note: The Fitzpatrick skin phototype rates skin by its reaction to sunlight, burning against tanning, and correlates the colour of skin with it; it was developed for white skin, and skin of colour was later divided into type IV (olive), V (brown) and VI (black) ({cite:taylor2002color}). What differs with pigment is the junction of epidermis and dermis: denser papillae in darker skin, and a slower loss of them with age ({cite:lagarrigue2012papilla}, {cite:querleux2009ethnic}). So the skin type sets the papillae of the junction shown with the selection, by age; the model's junction is flat and has no sun exposure, so it sets no model value (see {help:start/junction|The junction}). It is kept with the selection and colours the figure. The ethnicity suggests a skin type when it is chosen, from the types the sources report for that group ({cite:gambichler2006epidermis}, {cite:mercurio2016brazilian}, {cite:muizzuddin2010barrier}, {cite:chan2018asian}, {cite:ince2015dermal}, {cite:langton2019color}): III for European skin, the default. A skin type chosen afterwards stays.
